The stationary-Earth picture is the **geocentric** model, and its classical author is
**Ptolemy**.
**The Ptolemaic system.** Claudius Ptolemy, working in Alexandria in the second century
AD, set out in the *Almagest* a universe with the **Earth fixed at the centre** ✓ The
Sun, Moon, planets and stars were carried round it on a system of circles - **deferents**
carrying smaller circles called **epicycles**.
**Why it lasted fourteen centuries.** It **worked**, as a calculating device ✓ By adding
enough epicycles it predicted planetary positions well enough for calendars and
navigation, and it agreed with everyday experience: the ground does not feel as though it
moves.
**What the epicycles were for.** Planets sometimes appear to reverse their motion against
the stars - **retrograde motion** ✓ A planet carried on a small circle, itself carried on
a big one, can appear to loop backwards, which is how Ptolemy saved the appearances
without moving the Earth.
**Why it was eventually abandoned.** The model grew steadily more complicated as
observations improved. **Copernicus** (1543) put the Sun at the centre and explained
retrograde motion simply, as an effect of the Earth overtaking an outer planet ✓
**Kepler** then replaced the circles with ellipses, and **Newton** explained why.
**The others, and what they held.**
**Kepler** - three laws of **planetary motion about the Sun**, the opposite picture
**Galileo** - telescopic evidence **for** the Sun-centred system
**Newton** - universal gravitation, which explained the Sun-centred system ✓
None of the three held the Earth to be stationary.
∴ Ptolemy.

Among the four named, the Sun-centred planetary system belongs to **Kepler**.
**What Kepler established.** Johannes Kepler, working on Tycho Brahe's observations of
Mars, published three laws of planetary motion between 1609 and 1619, all of them with
the **Sun at rest and the planets going round it** ✓
**first law** - each planet moves in an **ellipse** with the Sun at one focus
**second law** - the line from Sun to planet sweeps **equal areas in equal times**
**third law** - T² ∝ a³, the square of the period against the cube of the semi-major
axis ✓
Each law is stated **about the Sun**, so the Sun-centred frame is built into them.
**The historical sequence.** **Copernicus** proposed the heliocentric idea in 1543, but
kept circular orbits and still needed epicycles ✓ Kepler replaced the circles with
ellipses, which made the model accurate for the first time; it is his version that
survives. Copernicus is not among the options, so Kepler is the figure who holds this
position here.
**How the others relate to it.**
**Galileo** - gathered the **evidence**: the moons of Jupiter, the phases of Venus, the
mountains of the Moon ✓ He defended the Sun-centred system rather than postulating it.
**Newton** - **explained** it, by deriving Kepler's three laws from the inverse-square
law of gravitation ✓
**Ptolemy** - held the opposite, Earth-centred, view.
**Why Kepler's laws still matter.** They apply unchanged to artificial satellites, to the
Moon about the Earth and to binary stars ✓ The third law is how the mass of a central
body is measured, from the period and radius of anything orbiting it.
∴ Keplar.

Judge the assertion and the reason separately, then ask whether the reason **explains**
the assertion.
**Step 1 — test the assertion.** Of the forces met in a physics course, the nuclear force
has by far the **shortest range** ✓
gravitational: **infinite** range, falling as 1/r²
electromagnetic: **infinite** range, falling as 1/r²
nuclear (strong): effective only within about **10⁻¹⁵ m**, and falling away
exponentially beyond it ✓
So the assertion is **true**.
**Step 2 — test the reason.** Because its reach is about the size of a nucleus, the
nuclear force binds the protons and neutrons of a nucleus and does nothing outside it ✓
So the reason is also a **true** statement.
**Step 3 — ask whether the reason explains the assertion.** It does not. "Operates within
the nucleus only" is a **consequence** of the short range, not a cause of it ✓ The
logic runs the other way: the force has a short range, **therefore** it acts only within
the nucleus. Offering the consequence as the explanation reverses cause and effect.
**What would count as an explanation.** The strong force is mediated by **massive**
exchange particles (pions, and at a deeper level gluons in a confined field), and a
massive mediator gives a force that dies away exponentially over a distance ℏ/mc ✓ That
is why the range is short. The photon, being massless, gives the electromagnetic force
its infinite range.
**Why the short range matters.** It explains why nuclei cannot grow indefinitely large ✓
The nuclear attraction reaches only to neighbouring nucleons, while the electrostatic
repulsion between protons acts across the whole nucleus - so beyond about Z = 83 the
repulsion wins and nuclei become unstable.
**Step 4 — match to the options.** Both statements true, but the reason is not the
correct explanation ✓
∴ B.

Here the assertion holds but the reason misstates the range of the weak force.
**Step 1 — test the assertion.** The weak nuclear force governs **beta decay** and the
decays of many unstable elementary particles ✓ Its characteristic interactions involve
short-lived particles - muons, pions, kaons, and the neutrons and nuclei that undergo
beta decay - so the assertion is **true**.
**Step 2 — test the reason.** The weak force does **not** operate over "a range of
nuclear size" ✓ Its range is about **10⁻¹⁸ m**, roughly **a thousand times smaller**
than a nucleus (about 10⁻¹⁵ m). It is the **strong** nuclear force whose range is of
nuclear size. So the reason is **false**.
**Step 3 — match to the options.** The assertion is true and the reason is false ✓
**Why the weak range is so tiny.** A force's range is set by the **mass** of the particle
that carries it, as ℏ/mc ✓ The weak force is mediated by the **W and Z bosons**, which
weigh about 80 to 91 GeV/c² - some ninety times the mass of a proton. Such heavy
mediators give an extraordinarily short reach. The strong force's pions, at 140 MeV/c²,
are far lighter, which is why its range is a thousand times greater.
**The four forces, by range and strength.**
**strong**: strongest, range ~10⁻¹⁵ m
**electromagnetic**: about 1/137 of the strong force, **infinite** range
**weak**: about 10⁻¹³ of the strong force, range ~10⁻¹⁸ m ✓
**gravitational**: weakest by far, ~10⁻³⁹, **infinite** range
**Why the weak force matters despite its feebleness.** It is the only force that can
change one kind of quark into another ✓ Without it there would be no beta decay, no
hydrogen fusion in the Sun's core, and no sunlight.
∴ C.

The scientist tried and punished for his astronomical views was **Galileo Galilei**.
**What happened.** Galileo's telescopic observations from 1609 - the **four moons of
Jupiter**, the **phases of Venus**, sunspots and lunar mountains - supported the
Sun-centred system of Copernicus ✓ He argued the case publicly, most forcefully in his
*Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems* (1632).
**The trial.** In 1633 the Roman Inquisition tried him for holding a doctrine then judged
contrary to scripture ✓ He was made to **recant**, his book was banned, and he spent the
last nine years of his life under **house arrest** at Arcetri, where he went blind.
**Why the phases of Venus mattered so much.** In Ptolemy's model Venus could never show
a **full** phase, because it would always lie between the Earth and the Sun ✓ Galileo saw
the full cycle of phases, which the Earth-centred model could not accommodate. It was
observation, not speculation, that made his case dangerous.
**What he was "punished for spreading".** From the point of view of his judges, a wrong
concept; from ours, a correct one ✓ That irony is the point of the question - scientific
truth is not settled by authority.
**The sequel.** Galileo's work on falling bodies and inertia, written during that
confinement in *Two New Sciences*, became the foundation Newton built on ✓ In 1992 the
Church formally acknowledged that the judgment had been in error.
**The others.** **Kepler**, **Ptolemy** and **Newton** ✗ were never tried or punished
for their scientific views; Newton in particular was honoured in his lifetime and buried
in Westminster Abbey ✓
∴ Galileo.
